E9 – FET Physics: JFET, MOSFET and CMOS (T8, Week 6)

Why this matters in the exam: Test 1 covered Weeks 1–5 only, so FETs are new material for the final, and the final is expected to weight FETs and Weeks 6–10. There is no past final paper in your files, so the best evidence is the course itself. WS7 (this week’s workshop) is 7 short calculation and sketch questions, and Weeks 7–8 build straight on top of them. Every JFET and D-MOSFET bias question in Week 7 (fixed-bias, self-bias, voltage-divider, common-gate) starts by sketching the transfer curve with the and points from this pack. Expect a few marks for a direct Shockley or calculation, and expect these same steps to sit inside every larger FET bias question.

1. The core ideas

1.2 JFET construction and operation (slides 8–15)

An n-channel JFET is an n-type bar (the channel) between drain and source, with p-type gate regions on both sides. The gate–channel pn junctions are always reverse biased in normal use, so the gate draws no current.

  • , rising from 0: the channel acts as a resistor, so rises roughly linearly. The drain end is more reverse biased than the source end, so the depletion regions are wider near the drain.
  • Pinch-off: at (with ) the two depletion regions almost touch. Past this point stays at a constant level. The JFET then acts as a current source.
  • = drain current with gate shorted to source () and . It is the maximum drain current of a JFET.
  • : the depletion regions widen, the channel narrows, and the saturation current drops below .
  • : the channel is closed. (cut-off). Datasheets often call (slide 11).
  • Ohmic (voltage-controlled resistance) region: left of the pinch-off locus. Resistance rises as goes more negative:

  • Pinch-off locus (Boylestad, consistent with the slides): the knee of each curve sits at . For this gives , matching slide 10.

1.3 Shockley’s equation (slides 16–19)

  • What: the transfer curve ( vs ) of a JFET or a depletion MOSFET in the saturation (pinch-off) region.
  • When: any time you are given and and need from (or the reverse), and to sketch the transfer curve.
  • Trap: and carry their signs. For an n-channel device both are negative, so is positive and less than 1. If you drop a sign you get and a current above , which a JFET cannot have.
  • Trap: it only holds for in saturation and for between and 0 (JFET). Outside the answer is , not the value the parabola gives.

1.5 MOSFET types (slides 21–31)

Device Channel at ? Equation Operating (n-channel) p-channel version
JFET Yes Shockley ,
Depletion MOSFET (D-MOSFET) Yes (built in) Shockley, both sides of : depletion mode. : enhancement mode, . Positive depletes, negative enhances
Enhancement MOSFET (E-MOSFET) No for , else , needs
  • The SiO layer insulates the gate from the channel. That gives the MOSFET its very high input impedance (slide 22).
  • D-MOSFET: is no longer the maximum current. Positive draws extra electrons from the p-substrate into the channel (slide 24 drain characteristics).
  • E-MOSFET: there is no channel until reaches the threshold (datasheets: ). A positive gate voltage pulls electrons up to the oxide and induces an n-channel (slide 29). Saturation starts at

  • Trap: the E-MOSFET does not use Shockley’s equation and has no (slide 28).

1.8 Sign conventions for p-channel devices (slides 13, 26, 31, 52–53)

Everything flips:

  • Doping is reversed (p-channel, n-type gate or substrate) and the carriers are holes.
  • is positive for a p-JFET (slide 13: mA, V) and for a p-channel D-MOSFET. is negative for a p-channel E-MOSFET.
  • is negative, and conventional current flows from source to drain. Most questions quote as a magnitude.
  • The equations keep the same form. Substitute the signed values: with , and with .
  • In the symbols, the gate (JFET) or substrate (MOSFET) arrow points in for n-channel and out for p-channel.
  • pMOS in a CMOS inverter: the source is at , so (slide 53).

1.9 The inverter and CMOS (slides 38–53)

Logic levels. Logic 0 is . Logic 1 is . Values in between are undefined.

VTC (voltage transfer characteristic) = vs . It is approximated by three straight lines: flat at up to , a falling transition (amplifier) region from to , then flat at .

Symbol Meaning (slide 47 table)
, Output low and high levels
Maximum input still read as logic 0
Minimum input still read as logic 1
Noise margin for a low input
Noise margin for a high input

Noise margin logic (slides 46–47). Noise adds to the line between gate and gate : . If outputs , still reads 0 as long as . That gives . The high case gives the same way.

Ideal VTC (slide 45): , and . That gives , the largest possible. The vertical transition means infinite gain if the inverter were used as an amplifier.

Implementation (slides 48–49).

  • Resistor plus switch: the “on” switch has a finite , so is not exactly 0.
  • Complementary pull-up (PU) and pull-down (PD) switches: exactly one is on, so and . This is the basis of CMOS.

CMOS inverter (slides 51–53). The pMOS (, source at ) sits on top and the nMOS (, source at ground) underneath. The gates are tied together as and the drains are tied together as . Both are enhancement MOSFETs.

nMOS pMOS
0 V 0 V −5 V Off On +5 V
+5 V +5 V 0 V On Off 0 V

In either logic state one transistor is off, so almost no current flows from to ground. That is why CMOS uses very little power. It also has high input impedance and fast switching (slide 51).

Propagation delay (slide 50). Feed the inverter an ideal pulse and measure each delay from the input edge to the moment the output crosses :

  • : delay for the output going high to low.
  • : delay for the output going low to high.

4. Traps that cost marks

  • Losing the sign in Shockley. V with V gives , not . A JFET answer above means you dropped a sign. Only a D-MOSFET with positive may exceed .
  • Using Shockley past pinch-off. For a JFET with beyond (e.g. −7 V with V), . The parabola would rise again, which is wrong.
  • Using Shockley or for an E-MOSFET. It has no . Use and set below .
  • Keeping the wrong root. has two roots, and only one gives an on device. Shockley’s inverse has the same issue: if you solve the quadratic by hand, a root with must be rejected.
  • unit mix-ups. Writing then using in A gives an answer that is wrong by a factor of 1000. Write mA/V explicitly.
  • p-channel signs. A p-JFET has , and a pMOS in CMOS has , not . Using for the pMOS gets the whole CMOS table wrong.
  • Noise-margin swap. and . Remember that each margin is the gap on the same side of the VTC: low with low, high with high.
  • Sketching a straight line or wrong curvature. The transfer curve is a parabola, concave up, that touches the axis at . A straight line from to would pass through at instead of .

7. Add to your open-book reference sheet

FET PHYSICS (Week 6)                         I_G = 0  ->  I_S = I_D
JFET / D-MOSFET (Shockley, saturation):
  I_D = I_DSS (1 - VGS/VP)^2       VGS = VP (1 - sqrt(I_D/I_DSS))
  I_DSS: VGS = 0, VDS >= |VP|  (max for JFET; D-MOSFET can exceed with VGS>0)
  JFET: I_D = 0 for VGS beyond VP (VP = VGS(off))
  Sketch: (0, I_DSS) (0.3VP, I_DSS/2) (VP/2, I_DSS/4) (VP, 0)  concave up
  Ohmic: r_d = r_o / (1 - VGS/VP)^2     Knee: VDS(sat) = VGS - VP
E-MOSFET:
  I_D = k (VGS - VT)^2  for VGS > VT (n), else 0      no I_DSS!
  k = I_D(on) / (VGS(on) - VGS(Th))^2   [mA/V^2]
  VGS = VT +/- sqrt(I_D/k): keep the root that turns it ON
  VDS(sat) = VGS - VT
p-CHANNEL: same equations, signed values.
  p-JFET, p-DMOS: VP > 0.  p-EMOS: VT < 0, on for VGS < VT.  VDS < 0.
OUTPUT char = I_D vs VDS (VGS steps).  TRANSFER = I_D vs VGS (in saturation).
  Output -> transfer: read I_D at each VGS at one saturation VDS.
INVERTER / CMOS:
  NM_L = V_IL - V_OL     NM_H = V_OH - V_IH
  Ideal: V_OH = VDD, V_OL = 0, V_IL = V_IH = VDD/2 -> NM = VDD/2
  CMOS: VGS,n = Vi ; VGS,p = Vi - VDD.  Vi=0 -> pMOS on, Vo=VDD; Vi=VDD -> nMOS on, Vo=0
  One device always off -> ~no static power
  t_P = (t_PLH + t_PHL)/2, each measured to the output crossing VDD/2
